subject: religious-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: For Kant, an action has genuine moral worth when it is done:
options: From duty, out of respect for the moral law
questions.explain: Kant holds that only actions performed from duty, for the sake of the moral law itself, have moral worth.

questions.q: What kind of argument is Anselm's ontological argument?
options: A posteriori and synthetic, based on observation
A priori and analytic, based on the concept of God alone
questions.explain: The ontological argument is a priori and analytic, deducing God's existence from the definition of God rather than from experience.

questions.q: Joseph Fletcher's Situation Ethics holds that the single intrinsically good thing is:
questions.explain: Fletcher argued that agape (selfless, unconditional Christian love) is the one absolute, and rightness is determined by what best serves love.

questions.q: In meta-ethics, cognitivism is the view that moral statements:
options: Merely express emotions and have no truth value
Are propositions that can be true or false
questions.explain: Cognitivism holds that ethical statements assert facts and are capable of being true or false.

questions.q: In business ethics, the principle that a company has obligations beyond shareholders to employees, consumers and the wider community is known as:
questions.explain: Corporate social responsibility holds that businesses bear duties toward a range of stakeholders, not just maximising shareholder profit.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of Aquinas's five primary precepts?
questions.explain: Aquinas's primary precepts are preservation of life, reproduction, education of the young, living in society (ordered society), and worshipping God.

questions.q: The Euthyphro dilemma, often raised against the moral argument, asks:
options: Whether something is good because God commands it, or God commands it because it is good
Whether the universe had a beginning
questions.explain: The Euthyphro dilemma challenges divine command theory by asking whether morality is arbitrary (good because commanded) or independent of God.

questions.q: In Aquinas's doctrine of analogy, when we say 'God is good', the term 'good' is used:
options: Univocally, in exactly the same sense as for humans
Analogically, neither identical to nor wholly different from its human use
questions.explain: Aquinas argues religious language works by analogy (of attribution and proportion), avoiding both univocal and purely equivocal meaning.

questions.q: Moore's intuitionism claims that the property of goodness is known by:
questions.explain: For Moore, 'good' is non-natural and grasped directly by intuition rather than defined or empirically observed.

questions.q: How does Anselm define God in the first form of his ontological argument in the Proslogion?
options: The uncaused cause of the universe
The designer of the natural world
That than which nothing greater can be conceived
questions.explain: Anselm defines God as 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived', arguing such a being must exist in reality, not merely in the mind.

questions.q: What is the role of Plato's Demiurge in the Timaeus?
options: To embody the Form of the Good in human form
To create matter ex nihilo from nothing
To fashion the cosmos by imposing order on pre-existing chaotic matter using the Forms as a model
questions.explain: The Demiurge is a craftsman who shapes already-existing matter according to the eternal Forms, rather than creating from nothing.

questions.q: Which of these is one of Hume's criticisms of the design argument?
options: The universe must have a first cause
The world is more like a living organism or a vegetable than a designed machine, weakening the analogy
questions.explain: Hume challenges the design analogy, suggesting the universe might resemble an organism that grows rather than an artefact that is made.

questions.q: A natural law approach to voluntary euthanasia would most likely judge it wrong because it:
options: Violates the primary precept of preserving life
Is not the most loving option
questions.explain: Natural Law upholds the preservation of life as a primary precept, so deliberately ending life conflicts with that basic good.

questions.q: A Kantian objection to a business deceiving customers for profit appeals chiefly to the idea that the firm:
options: Cultivates a vice rather than a virtue
Treats customers merely as means to an end
questions.explain: Deception uses people merely as instruments for profit, violating Kant's formula of humanity that persons be treated as ends.

questions.q: How does Plato's view of the soul's relationship to the body differ from Aristotle's?
options: Plato sees the soul as immortal and separable, imprisoned in the body; Aristotle sees the soul as the form of the body
Both regard the soul as identical to brain activity
Plato sees the soul as the form of the body; Aristotle sees it as a separable substance
Both deny the existence of any soul
questions.explain: Plato's dualism treats the soul as a distinct immortal substance, whereas Aristotle treats the soul as the form/animating principle of a living body.

questions.q: Which is a recognised challenge to the reliability of religious experience?
options: Naturalistic explanations from psychology (e.g. Freud) and neuroscience suggesting internal causes
questions.explain: Critics argue religious experiences may be products of psychological need or brain states rather than genuine encounters with God.

questions.q: Situation Ethics is best classified as a theory that is:
questions.explain: Situation Ethics is teleological (judging by the loving end) and relativist (rules may be set aside to serve agape).

questions.q: The via negativa (apophatic way) approaches language about God by:
options: Saying only what God is not, since God transcends human description
questions.explain: The via negativa preserves God's transcendence by denying limiting human attributes, asserting only what God is not.

questions.q: Aquinas's conscientia refers to:
options: The innate orientation toward the good
A faculty that is always infallible
Reason making particular moral decisions and applying principles
questions.explain: Conscientia is the activity of reason applying the principles of synderesis to specific situations, and it can err.

questions.q: A central claim of Augustine's theodicy is that:
options: Evil is a privation (privatio boni), a lack of good, originating in the misuse of free will at the Fall
God deliberately created evil for soul-making
Evil is a substance created by God
questions.explain: Augustine holds that evil is not a thing but a privation of good, entering creation through the free fall of angels and humans.

questions.q: Aquinas's Third Way (from contingency and necessity) concludes that there must exist:
options: A necessary being whose existence does not depend on anything else
questions.explain: The Third Way argues that contingent beings cannot account for their own existence, so a necessary being must exist to ground them.

questions.q: The first formulation of Kant's categorical imperative, the formula of universal law, states that one should:
options: Act only on a maxim you could will to become a universal law
Follow the loving thing to do in each situation
Treat the consequences as the measure of duty
Always maximise happiness for the greatest number
questions.explain: The universalisability formula requires acting only on maxims that could consistently be willed as universal laws without contradiction.

questions.q: Rudolf Otto's term 'numinous' refers to an experience of:
options: A non-rational sense of awe before a 'mysterium tremendum et fascinans', a holy 'wholly other'
questions.explain: The numinous is the felt sense of a holy, awe-inspiring and fascinating divine presence wholly distinct from the self.

questions.q: What is the central claim of Plantinga's free-will defence?
options: It is logically possible that God could not create a world with genuine moral good without the possibility of moral evil
questions.explain: The free-will defence argues that significant free will, which is valuable, makes the possibility of moral evil unavoidable even for an omnipotent God.

questions.q: Kant's categorical imperative is categorical because it:
options: Commands unconditionally, regardless of one's desires or goals
Depends on the consequences of an action
questions.explain: A categorical imperative binds absolutely and unconditionally, unlike a hypothetical imperative that depends on a desired end.

questions.q: What objection did J.S. Mill raise against the design argument?
options: That language about God is meaningless
That the cruelty and waste in nature count against a benevolent designer
That God is the greatest conceivable being
questions.explain: Mill argued that nature commits acts of horror and suffering that no good designer would be expected to produce.

questions.q: Freud's account of conscience locates it in the:
questions.explain: For Freud, conscience is a function of the super-ego, formed by internalised parental and societal authority rather than reason or God.

questions.q: Which is one of Fletcher's four working principles in Situation Ethics?
questions.explain: The four working principles are pragmatism, relativism, positivism and personalism.

questions.q: In Aquinas's Natural Law, the precepts that are universal and self-evident, derived from the rational nature of human purpose, are known as the:
questions.explain: Primary precepts are the unchanging, self-evident goals that flow from human nature, such as preserving life and reproducing.

questions.q: Which statement best characterises the materialist view of the mind?
options: The mind is the form of the body but survives death
Mental states are nothing over and above physical states of the brain and body
The mind is an immaterial substance separable from the body
The soul pre-exists the body and is immortal
questions.explain: Materialism holds that the mind is not a separate substance but is identical to, or wholly dependent on, physical brain states.
